findings.summary: The 'Inspecting It' flow is a flat list of fragments (head, look, info, types, nulls, describe, spread, isna().sum(), gaps) with no visible pairing, so a learner can't tell which word is the call and which is its purpose.
findings.evidence:
head
look
info
types, nulls
describe
spread
isna().sum()
gaps
findings.fix: Render it as a left-to-right chain such as head() → info() → describe() → isna().sum(), with each step's purpose under it. Or drop it, because the table below already covers the same calls.

findings.summary: The loc/iloc comparison row has a cryptic label and packs two results into one table cell.
findings.fix: Rename the row to 'Rows returned by [0:2] (default index 0..n-1)' and write the cells as '3 rows' and '2 rows'. Drop the unrelated df[...] prefix.

findings.summary: A worked example uses a library that is not installed here, so its output was not checked.
findings.evidence: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'
findings.fix: Check the output by running it with the library installed.

findings.summary: astype('Int64') is described as allowing NaN, but the nullable integer dtype stores pd.NA, not NaN.
findings.evidence: astype('Int64') | nullable int, allows NaN (capital I)
findings.fix: Write: "nullable int; missing values are stored as <NA> (pd.NA). A float NaN is converted to <NA>, but fractional values raise."

findings.summary: The 'On bad value' column holds a description rather than a bad-value outcome in the astype('Int64') row, and the 'same, errors=coerce' row has no call named.
findings.evidence:
astype('Int64') | nullable int, allows NaN (capital I)
same, errors='coerce' | NaN / NaT
findings.fix: Make the astype('Int64') cell 'raises on non-numeric text; NaN allowed' and move 'nullable int' to a bullet. Write the coerce row as 'to_numeric / to_datetime(errors="coerce") | NaN / NaT'.

findings.summary: Terms for the text dtype are inconsistent across pages: page 1 says 'str in pandas 3, object before', page 3 says 'object', and page 4 says 'string'.
findings.evidence: Page 3: 'Mixed values in a column → object'. Page 4: 'The dtype is not string; use astype(\'string\')'. Page 1: 'A text dtype (str in pandas 3, object before)'.
findings.fix: Use one name for text columns throughout, noting once that it is str in pandas 3 and object before. Explain how astype('string') relates to str.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "whitespace", "collapses").
findings.evidence: s.str.replace('old','new', regex=False) is a literal replace; regex=True uses patterns, e.g. s.str.replace(r'\s+',' ', regex=True) collapses whitespace
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The Mistakes bullet 'Missing values return NaN, no error' does not say what goes wrong or why it counts as a mistake.
findings.evidence: Missing values return NaN, no error
findings.fix: State the consequence, for example 'NaN in the Series makes str.contains return NaN, which breaks boolean masks; pass na=False'.

findings.summary: The 'Python calls' column in the speed table is filled with a speed note, not a call count.
findings.evidence: map(dict) | fast lookup | fast
findings.fix: Write 'map(dict) | one dict lookup per element, in C | fast'.

findings.summary: In the Missing and Types section, call/purpose pairs are written as alternating one-line items, so a skimmer cannot tell which line is the call and which is its meaning.
findings.evidence:
isna().sum()
count
dropna(subset=, thresh=)
drop
fillna(value | median)
fill
ffill()
neighbour
findings.fix: Render these as a two-column table (Call | Does), for example 'isna().sum() | count missing per column'.

findings.summary: The outline's interview point for this section is missing, so the chapter never explains why groupby is lazy.
findings.evidence: Page 1 says "No data is computed at that point" and ends with "Remember: groupby alone computes nothing". It has no Interview Point section and gives no reason for the laziness.
findings.fix: Add an Interview Point block covering the three steps, why groupby is lazy (it defers work until an aggregation, transform, apply or iteration so the whole operation can run in one pass), and the shape each apply type returns.

findings.summary: A bullet about the result's shape is placed under the laziness heading, before the code that produces it.
findings.evidence: "One row per group, indexed by the key" sits under "GroupBy Is Lazy", just before the python sum example.
findings.fix: Move it to the caption of the sum example ("Series indexed by city") or drop it, and state the idea before the code.

findings.summary: The "Keys, Column, Aggregation" section mixes three unrelated options in one list, and an orphan label appears with no content under it.
findings.evidence: "Two keys give a MultiIndex result / as_index=False keeps the keys as columns / .reset_index() turns the keys back into columns" and the stray line "Different functions per column" above the final callout.
findings.fix: Group the as_index and reset_index bullets as "Keys back as columns". Remove the stray label or attach it to the named-aggregation callout.

findings.summary: The page title promises a comparison with apply, but apply is never explained, so the three-way comparison is incomplete.
findings.evidence: Title "transform vs agg vs apply"; the table only has "agg | transform" columns, and apply appears only in "a lambda or apply runs Python per group".
findings.fix: Add an apply column to the table (flexible output shape, runs Python per group, slowest), or rename the page "transform vs agg".

findings.summary: Two table rows say the same thing, which adds noise to a skim.
findings.evidence: "Output | one scalar per group | same length as df" and "Rows | one per group | same as df"
findings.fix: Delete the Rows row or merge it into Output.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "multiindex", "interview").
findings.evidence: Interview Point: Why can group counts not match the row count? How would you speed up a slow groupby? What does a MultiIndex result need to become flat columns?
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The outline's interview points for Common Mistakes are missing, including how to flatten a MultiIndex result.
findings.evidence: Page 5 has only the sections "Counts That Disagree", "Wrong or Slow Aggregation" and "Fix Summary". Nothing says what a MultiIndex result needs in order to become flat columns.
findings.fix: Add an Interview Point block. It should say why group counts differ from the row count (NaN keys, count vs size), how to speed up a slow groupby (built-in names, select columns first), and that a MultiIndex result needs reset_index() or as_index=False to become flat columns.

findings.summary: The count versus size NaN rule is written as a bullet and then repeated as a table, and one section mixes two separate causes under "Counts That Disagree".
findings.evidence: "count() skips NaN values; size() counts all rows" followed by the Call | Counts | NaN table; the same section also holds "groupby drops NaN keys by default".
findings.fix: Keep the table and drop the duplicate bullet. Split the NaN-key point into its own bullet or row.

findings.summary: The "Interview Point" heading sits over a plain tool-selection table with no questions in it, and the heading is used inconsistently with pages 2 and 3.
findings.evidence: "3. Interview Point: Pick the Tool" followed by a Tool | Returns table.
findings.fix: Rename it "Pick the Tool" or rewrite it as question and answer lines like pages 2 and 3.

findings.summary: The outline's interview question on when long format beats wide is never answered.

findings.summary: The code block lists four calls with no comments, and the single output table is not tied to a specific call, so a skimmer cannot tell which line produces it.
findings.evidence:
s.unstack()
s.unstack(fill_value=0)
s.loc[('a1','b1')]
s.xs('b1', level='b')
...a b1 b2 / a1 1.0 2.0 / a2 3.0 NaN
findings.fix: Add a one-line comment to each call. Label the table as the result of s.unstack() and note that fill_value=0 turns NaN into 0.

findings.summary: The cheat sheet writes validate='1:1' while pages 2 and 6 name the same option values 'one_to_one' and 'one_to_many', with no link between the two spellings.
findings.evidence: Page 2: "validate='one_to_one', 'one_to_many', 'many_to_one'"; page 6: "validate='1:1' raises on bad keys"
findings.fix: Use one spelling throughout, or note once on page 2 that '1:1' is the alias for 'one_to_one'.

findings.summary: The Timedelta row of the type table is a cut-off fragment.
findings.evidence: "Timedelta | difference of two | timedelta64[unit]"
findings.fix: Write "difference between two Timestamps".

findings.summary: One bullet holds two ideas.
findings.evidence: "NaT propagates through arithmetic; most aggregations skip it"
findings.fix: Split into two bullets: one for arithmetic propagation, one for aggregations skipping NaT.

findings.summary: The slicing code comes before the idea behind it, and the section mixes slicing with grouping keys.
findings.evidence: "3. Slicing and grouping keys" opens straight with df.loc['2024'] ... and only afterwards says "sorted DatetimeIndex; both ends inclusive"
findings.fix: Put the one-line rule first (partial strings slice a sorted DatetimeIndex, both ends inclusive), then the code. Split grouping keys and between_time into their own section.

findings.summary: The rule for date_range arguments is imprecise and could be misread.
findings.evidence: "Give any two of start, end, periods"
findings.fix: Say that date_range needs three of start, end, periods and freq, and that freq defaults to 'D'.

findings.summary: The shift and pct_change code is shown before its one-line idea, and the lag, lead and change calls are only comments.
findings.evidence: "3. Lag, lead, change" goes straight to the code block, and the summary "s.pct_change() == s / s.shift(1) - 1, first row NaN" comes after it.
findings.fix: Open with the one-line idea (shift moves values, pct_change is a ratio, diff is a difference), and show the code after it. Alternatively use a Call | Gives table like the cheat sheet.

findings.summary: Two lines on the page contradict each other about calling tz_localize on aware data.

findings.fix: Reword to "tz_localize('zone') on aware data raises TypeError; only tz_localize(None) works on aware data", or fold both cases into the table.
